metadata.title: Every Image Earns Its Place
metadata.greeting_note: ATTRIBUTION OVERRIDE (established 2026-07-31, carried forward): hosted by Sai in his own name, not by Liam-in-for-Bear. Voice stays Kokoro am_onyx. B00 says 'this is Sai'; B08 signs off 'Sai.' The IN-FOR-BEAR LAW of WEEKLY-VIDEO-GUIDE.md is deliberately suspended for this series — see PEDAGOGY.md.
metadata.note: WEEKLY PROGRESS REEL for the loon-detector project (National Loon Center / 'Immer'), week of 2026-08-21. Not a concept explainer — this is the 8-beat weekly-progress spine of WEEKLY-VIDEO-GUIDE.md, extended to five body beats. THE WEEK, as reported by the author: (1) a centralized repository so every loon image lives in one place, (2) a script with two halves — a quality gate (sharpness floor + resolution/altitude floor) and a duplicate check (EXACT FILE HASH ONLY), (3) a Lovable mock of the Immer user flow, used as an internal demo. THROUGH-LINE: before you train anything you decide what is allowed in, and you write that decision down as code. DOUBLE-CHECK LAW — THIS REEL CARRIES NO FIGURES. The author confirmed he has no real counts this week, so nothing numeric is asserted anywhere: no image counts, no reject rates, no dedupe totals. B02's gate is described by KIND of check (sharp / big enough), never by threshold value, because the actual threshold numbers were not supplied. The two screenshot plates (B04, B05) do contain Lovable's placeholder figures (1,248 images, 387 loons, 68% annotation); B05's narration says out loud that every figure on that screen is a placeholder, and the plate itself is captioned 'MOCK DATA · EVERY FIGURE ON THIS SCREEN IS A PLACEHOLDER'. HONEST LIMIT, stated rather than hidden: exact hashing catches a re-uploaded file, not burst frames or the same bird on a second pass — B03 is built around that gap instead of implying the dedupe is finished. ILLUSTRATE LAW: Claude UI at B00, B06, B07, B08 only; the five body beats are DivergentFates -> BinaryBranch -> ChipGrid -> STILL -> STILL, no two consecutive Remotion patterns repeated. The two consecutive stills are a deliberate two-shot walkthrough of one artifact and are differentiated by motion (ken burns, then hold). SHORTS: every Remotion pattern used here has a registered *916 portrait sibling, so shorts.py rewires the whole reel with no new TSX; the two STILL beats are covered by hand-composed pantry/<bid>-916.png plates so they are never centre-cut. BRANDING RULE 7: slot-1 kicker stays 'Computational Skepticism'.

beats.narration_text: The model is not the hard part yet. First somebody has to decide which images are allowed to become training data, and write that decision down. This is Sai. Three things this week: one place for the images, a script that guards the door, and a mock of the app.

props.command: We are building a loon detector from drone and field imagery. Before any training happens, I want the dataset itself to be defensible. Give me one place the images live, a script that decides what is allowed in, and something the team can click through to see where this is going.
output: one repository — every loon image in one location, one known shape
one script, two gates — is it worth training on, and have we seen it before
one mock — the Immer user flow, clickable, for the team to react to

beats.narration_text: First, a centralized repository. Every loon image now lives in one place, with one known shape. That sounds like housekeeping. It is not. A set scattered across laptops and shared drives has no answer to the question that matters later: which images did we actually train on?

the split marker: where does an image land when it arrives?
the scattered track bends down — copies drift, nobody can name the set
the single-repository track climbs
both endpoints badge: a set you can name, versus a set you can only guess at

beats.narration_text: Then the first half of the script: is this image worth training on? Right now that is two mechanical questions. Is it sharp enough, not smeared by drone motion. And is it big enough, shot close enough that the bird is more than a few grey pixels.

two branches draw down — admitted on one side, rejected on the other
each card carries what the check actually looks at
the ghost line surfaces: a rejected image is cheap, a bad one is not
the resolver lands in terracotta — the floors live in the script, not in memory

beats.narration_text: The second half is duplicates, and today it compares the file itself. That catches the same file uploaded twice, which is the common case. It does not catch two frames of one burst, or the same bird on a second pass. Identical file, yes. Nearly identical picture, not yet.

beats.narration_text: Third: the app all of this feeds. This is Immer, mocked up in Lovable this week — a demo for ourselves, not a build. The promise is right on the front page. Every detection is reviewed by a researcher before it becomes data.

beats.narration_text: The week on one page. One place for the images. One script at the door, checking sharpness and size. Exact duplicates caught, the near ones still open. And a mock that shows where all of it is going. No model yet, and that is the right order.

props.artifactHeading: Loon detector · dataset week, one page
artifactLines: A centralized repository: every loon image in one location with one known shape, so that 'which images did we train on?' has an answer instead of an argument.
Gate one, quality: a sharpness floor and a resolution floor, applied before a human ever spends time labelling the frame. The rule lives in the script, not in somebody's judgement on the day.
Gate two, uniqueness: exact file hashing catches the re-uploaded file. Burst frames and the same bird on a second pass are not caught yet — and those are the ones that leak across a split.
A Lovable mock of the Immer flow — analyze, review, dataset — as an internal demo. Its figures are placeholders, not measurements. The shape is the deliverable, not the numbers.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take the dataset you are building and write down the rule that decides what gets in. Then run it over what you have already collected, and count what it throws away.

props.command: Take the training set I am collecting. Write the admission rule as code — the sharpness floor, the resolution floor, the duplicate check. Now run it over everything I have already gathered, show me what it rejects and why, and then tell me plainly what my rule still cannot catch.

beats.narration_text: Every image earns its place. Build the door before you build the model. Next week, the harder half: the near duplicates. Sai.
